B_source.statement: An [[Definition:Inductive Type|inductive type]] $\mu F$ is characterized by its constructors $\mathsf {in}: \map F {\mu F} \to \mu F$, and properties of its elements are proved by [[Principle of Structural Induction|induction]].

substitutions.the least fixed point of the signature: the greatest fixed point of the signature

derived.proving a property of all elements by in: proving two elements equal by exhibiting a bisimulation
derived.finiteness of constructed elements: possible infiniteness of observed elements, such as streams

object_map.reformulation: Reverse the direction of the defining maps, exchanging construction for observation and least for greatest fixed point.

validity_conditions: The two notions are related by reversing the arrows in the defining diagrams, exchanging the initial algebra with the terminal coalgebra.
Elements of an inductive type are finitely generated, whereas a coinductive type admits infinite elements such as streams, so termination arguments do not carry over.
Equality is the notion that dualizes: induction proves properties of a single element, while coinduction proves indistinguishability of two under all observations.
proof_plan: The [[Definition:Inductive Type|inductive type]] is the [[Definition:Initial Algebra|initial algebra]] $\mathsf {in}: \map F {\mu F} \to \mu F$, the [[Definition:Least Fixed Point|least fixed point]] of the signature $F$.

Reversing the arrows gives the [[Definition:Final Coalgebra|final coalgebra]] $\mathsf {out}: \nu F \to \map F {\nu F}$.
This is the [[Definition:Greatest Fixed Point|greatest fixed point]] of $F$, determined by its destructors.

Initiality gives the [[Principle of Structural Induction|induction principle]] and unique folds out of $\mu F$.
Finality gives unique unfolds into $\nu F$, and hence the [[Definition:Coinduction|coinduction]] principle.
